# doe-aion

> Watches the Department of Education's machine-readable sources, detects real
> change in **34 CFR** — all of Title 34, Education — and emits a
> cryptographically signed `.aion` chain.

## What this repository is

It reads Title 34 of the Code of Federal Regulations from eCFR at a pinned
date, reconstructs each section's paragraph tree, derives obligation atoms from
the regulatory prose, and signs the result. Released as `chain-vN` tags.

Current state: 108 live parts, 3,296 sections, 36,828 paragraphs, 18,088
obligation atoms of which 12,064 binding.

Title 34 includes **IDEA Part B (34 CFR 300)** and **Part C (34 CFR 303)**,
FERPA (part 99), the civil-rights parts (100, 104, 106, 110) and EDGAR
(parts 75–77, 81, 84, 86), alongside the Title IV student-aid parts (600–694).

## What you may and may not conclude from it

- **A signature proves provenance, not correctness.** The chain proves what this
  program read from eCFR on a given date and which key signed for it. It does
  **not** prove the reading was right, that the derived obligations are
  complete, or that a bearer was correctly identified.
- **The upstream source is not the official legal edition.** eCFR is an
  editorial compilation; the Administrative Committee of the Federal Register
  has not granted it official status, and until it does the compilation does not
  provide legal notice to the public or judicial notice to the courts. Verify
  against the official CFR, the Federal Register, and the LSA. A signed chain
  over an unofficial source is still an unofficial source, signed.
- **Not legal advice, and not a compliance determination.**
- **Coverage limits are inside the signed payload, deliberately.** As of
  `chain-v2`: 88 unresolved designator sequences across 36,828 paragraphs
  (0.24%), 5,841 atoms with an unclassified bearer (32.3%), 9 amendments
  published in the Federal Register but not yet incorporated into the text a
  pin retrieves.
- **`applicant` is a known ambiguity** — a student in Title IV, a grant
  applicant in the grants parts — and second-person `you` is defined per
  subpart and reported as `addressee` rather than guessed.

## The relationship to the other repositories

| repository | corpus | this repo's relation to it |
|---|---|---|
| `aion-context` | the `.aion` format and library | dependency |
| `selpa-aion` | Cal. Educ. Code Part 30 (special education) | **cites into this one** |
| `fedramp-aion` | FedRAMP, NIST 800-53, CISA KEV | sibling, same pattern, no data overlap |

### Being resolved into, from `selpa-aion`

California's Education Code cites 34 CFR in its own statutory text. 96 of
Part 30's 401 sections do so, and `selpa-aion` carries those citations in its
signed payload. To resolve one here:

1. `selpa-aion federal 56341 --json` yields e.g. `["34 CFR 300.308", "34 CFR 300.310"]`.
2. Take the part before the dot — `300`.
3. Read `data/part-300.json` in this repository.
4. Find the entry in `sections[]` whose `identifier` equals `300.308`.
5. Its `paragraphs[]` carry citations of the form `34 CFR 300.308(a)(1)`.

The two chains are signed independently and by design: neither vouches for the
other, and a joined answer is only as good as both signatures plus this
resolution step.

## Where the data is

- `doe.aion` — the signed chain. One payload, versioned.
- `registry.json` — public keys only. No private material is ever published.
- `data/part-<n>.json` — one file per live part, bound by digests inside the
  signed payload. Edit one and `doe-aion verify` fails.
- `data/ledger.json` — eCFR's amendment ledger, per section.
- Releases carry the chain, the registry, and all parts in one archive.

## Commands an agent can rely on

```sh
doe-aion verify --json           # structured verdict; exit 0 valid, 1 invalid
doe-aion part 300                # structure, pending amendments, unresolved sequences
doe-aion obligations 300 --json  # derived atoms with force, bearer, citation
doe-aion ledger --since 2026-07-01
```

`verify --json` reports `valid`, `version`, `pinned_date`, `bundle_sha256`, the
totals, **and** `unresolved`, `unclassified_bearer` and `pending_amendments`, so
a consumer can weigh the derivation's limits rather than discovering them later.

## One distinction that matters

`pending_amendments` counts changes eCFR has **published and not yet folded into
the text**. The regulation an institution reads today has not changed; the rule
that will change it exists. Reporting only one of those would be misleading, so
the artifact carries both.

## Reading order

1. `README.md` — the walk, with the measurements behind each decision
2. `DESIGN.md` — upstream behaviour, change-detection rules, determinism invariants
3. `src/cfr/paragraph.rs` — why `(i)` after `(h)` is not `(i)` after `(a)(1)`
4. `src/obligations.rs` — why `may not` is a prohibition and the Secretary is not the institution
